note: Two fixed offered rates, identical for every target in every language, published as real times rather than as a ratio to anything. The rates are chosen from the traffic a reader might want to serve, not from where the targets break: set from the population they would move every time a language is added, and moving them breaks the time series. 1000 and 5000 are provisional until the dedicated machine has run. docs/measurement-v2.html is the design.

warmup.note: serial_requests is the serial suite's equivalent of seconds. A rate ladder warms for a duration; a host that runs one invocation at a time warms for a count, and a JVM needs thousands of invocations to reach C2 rather than the few hundred a steady runtime needs.

rungs.name: regular
rungs.purpose: traffic every target is expected to serve; this is where latency is compared

rungs.name: raised
rungs.purpose: traffic that separates the frameworks with headroom from the ones without

abort.note: Watched during the settle window, which is unrecorded anyway. A target dropping this much twenty seconds in drops it four minutes in, so the remaining sample is spent to learn nothing. The settle doubles as the probe, so a target that passes pays nothing for the check.

publish.note: A blend is published only where the target completed the rate. gen/blend.mjs drops by never sending, so a dropped request never enters a histogram and the percentiles are computed over survivors: the requests excluded are the ones that would have been slowest, and a framework that collapses reports a better p99 than one that degrades gracefully. Where this is exceeded the row carries achieved rps and the drop count instead of a latency.

min_requests_note: What the ladder actually delivers, rather than a floor it has never met. Rung 1 is 1,000 rps for 240s, so 240,000 requests across 48 endpoints is 5,000 each; 10,000 was written when the set was smaller and the number was already half of it before the etag and cache families arrived. Lengthening the rung instead would have cost roughly five minutes a target a run and moved every published latency, because a longer rung is a different measurement. Set here so it is true, with room for about a dozen more endpoints before it binds. p99.9 rests on five observations per endpoint at this rate either way, which is what docs/measurement-v2.html says the raised rung is for.
